Whole-home surge protection

A surge protective device at your main panel protects everything wired to it: the air conditioning, the water heater and appliance controls, the garage door opener, and the electronics inside all of them. Paired with plug-in protection for TVs and computers, it covers the whole house.

What a surge protector at the panel does

Surges come from outside the house, from lightning and from switching on the utility’s lines, and from inside it, every time a large motor like the air conditioning compressor starts and stops. The big ones are rare. The small ones happen every day and wear down the circuit boards in appliances, HVAC controls and chargers over time.

A whole-home surge protective device mounts at the main panel and diverts a surge to ground before it travels out through your circuits. It works with plug-in surge strips, not instead of them: the panel device takes the large surges, and point-of-use protection handles what’s left at sensitive equipment.

Worth adding if

  • You’re replacing or upgrading your panel or service
  • You’re adding an EV charger, a generator or a new HVAC system
  • Electronics, chargers or appliance control boards have failed after a storm
  • The house has a variable-speed air conditioner, smart thermostat or other electronics-heavy equipment
  • There’s no surge protector at the panel now

At the panel and at the outlet

Whole-home, at the panel

  • Protects hardwired equipment a plug-in strip can’t reach: AC, water heater, garage door opener
  • Takes the large surges that arrive on the utility lines
  • Installed by a licensed electrician

Point-of-use, at the outlet

  • Plug-in protection for TVs, computers and networking gear
  • Handles smaller surges that start inside the house
  • Wears out over time; many show when protection is spent

Neither stops a direct lightning strike to the house. Together, they’re the practical protection.

  3. Install and confirm

    Power is off briefly while the device is connected. We confirm it shows protected before we leave.

Only as good as the grounding

A surge protector sends the surge to ground, so it depends on the grounding system behind it. Loose or corroded grounding connections are the first thing we look at, and we tell you if they need work.

Common questions

Is whole-home surge protection worth it?

For most houses, yes. It protects equipment a plug-in strip can’t reach, like the air conditioning, water heater controls, garage door opener and anything else that’s hardwired, and those are expensive to replace. It doesn’t replace plug-in protection for sensitive electronics; the two work together.

Will it protect against lightning?

No surge protector stops a direct strike to the house. A whole-home device handles surges that arrive through the utility lines, including those from lightning nearby, which is the far more common case.

Is surge protection required by code?

Under the current National Electrical Code, a surge protective device is required when a home’s service is installed or replaced, which includes most panel upgrades. Which code edition applies depends on your city or county; we check. Adding one to an existing panel is optional, and worth it.

Can you add it during a panel upgrade or generator install?

Yes, and that’s the easiest time, because we’re already working at the panel. On a service upgrade, current code requires it anyway. See panel upgrades and generator installation.
